title: Rodin’s Thinker began as ‘The Poet’, a small figure sitting above the Gates of Hell

cover.alt: Rodin’s bronze Thinker seen from below on a tall stone pedestal: a muscular nude man seated on a rock, chin resting on his hand, against a blue sky.

body: In 1880 Auguste Rodin took on a huge commission for a sculpted doorway, **The Gates of Hell**, based on Dante’s Divine Comedy. At the centre, over the doorway, sat a brooding nude figure first named The Poet, which some critics think was meant to be Dante himself contemplating his poem. The famous name came later, and so did the size: Rodin enlarged the 72 cm figure in 1902, the first monumental bronze was made in 1904, and a public subscription placed it in front of the Panthéon in Paris. Today there are more than two dozen full-size bronze casts.

slides.alt: Detail of Rodin’s Gates of Hell: the small seated Thinker, chin on hand, above a swirl of twisting nude figures.
slides.caption: Where it all started: the Thinker in his original place, above the doorway of The Gates of Hell at the Musée Rodin, among the doorway’s writhing figures.

slides.question: How tall was the figure when it sat on The Gates of Hell?
slides.explanation: About 72 cm. In 1902 Rodin had it enlarged to about 181 cm, the size of the famous monumental casts.

slides.heading: From doorway figure to monument
slides.note: Heights; the article gives about 181–185 cm for the big casts.

left.label: Yes
left.text: Some critics see Dante at the gates of Hell, thinking about the poem the doorway illustrates.

right.label: No
right.text: Others point out that Dante is always clothed in the poem, and that this muscular body doesn’t match his slighter build.

The original bronze moves to the Musée Rodin

slides.question: Who first called the figure ‘The Thinker’?
slides.explanation: Foundry workers did, because it reminded them of Michelangelo’s statue of Lorenzo de’ Medici, known as Il Pensieroso, ‘the thinker’.
